photographs.prompt:
Edit the FIRST input photograph. One full-bleed photographic image, wide 2.098:1, same camera and composition for a print gardening book. INPUT 1 is the base photograph for this exact first step. INPUT 2 is a three-view contact sheet of REAL CAMERA photographs of the man in the scene: very important for reshaping his jaw and chin faithfully. INPUT 3 supplies his actual cool-weather clothing only. This is one Cornish late-autumn afternoon, outdoors after a light shower, with cool overcast soft grey light, slight damp sheen on a few leaves and the tarp but no pouring rain or puddles. The picture will be paired with a warm sunny view taken the following late spring.
Keep John kneeling on the grass on the right, lowering the final brick onto the near right hem of a flat fully opaque, ordinary dark forest-green woven tarpaulin. Match his two hands on the brick, the ordinary perimeter weights, the existing layout and perspective of the tarp, his charcoal jumper, dark blue jeans and work shoes. Keep the fence, its worn low wall and the tiny slice at far right of his glass greenhouse on a pale grey brick plinth. Same understated, matter-of-fact photograph with comfortable headroom. NO shed.
The owner asks for a proper established lawn. REPLACE ALL the sparse, coarse and muddy ground visible OUTSIDE the edges of the tarp and under the actor with dense, closed, lush short mown lawn, attractive but authentic Cornish grass, mixed fine blades close together. A living continuous carpet with no earth peeking through it, right up to the tarpaulin, visible in front, along each side and behind. A few discreet recognisable flat dandelion, clover or plantain rosettes growing low in that lawn, especially near a tarp corner, testify to the weedy area, not an overgrown meadow. Leave the cover intact, flat and fully covering the treatment area with no dead weeds arranged on it. Subtle late-autumn clues only e.g. a couple of small fallen leaves at the fence, subdued greens; don't drown the details or darken the face.
Correct John's likeness using the real close views in the SECOND input as the authority. Match the slimmer taper in his lower cheeks, the small softly rounded and slightly set-back chin, his short mixed grey beard following his skin, softer natural jaw-to-neck transition. In particular bring back the protruding lower outline relative to the lower lip seen in the base, so it doesn't jut forward, square off, or appear reinforced by a shadow or by a thick block of beard. A relaxed mature man concentrating on the brick, still the same John, his natural forehead, hairline, nose and expression. Keep the downward gaze but let sufficient three-quarter part profile be seen to read the actual jaw contour. Understated documentary realism, normal texture, one image only, no typography or collage.

Make a careful photographic edit of reference 1, the complete reviewed garden photo. Change two coupled things: the man’s stance and the physical construction of the rake. Keep the intimate documentary landscape view and all of the approved garden details, late spring light and shadow, thin scruffy dead turf mat and irregular exposed soil with the fine brown fibres already in place. Same folded tarp, bricks, healthy surrounding lawn, rear fence and low wall, cropped greenhouse on its brick plinth at right. Same slightly oblique camera position. Reference 2 shows John's real face, including his soft gently rounded chin; reference 3 his olive T-shirt and shorts. Use him in those same spring clothes. Single full-bleed image, 2.098:1 landscape.
Direction: John is having a quiet potter in the garden. He has already done most of the job and is casually drawing a little loose thatch towards him. Photograph him in an EASY ALMOST UPRIGHT standing position on the right lawn edge, feet comfortably about 28–35 cm apart, nearly parallel, just one foot half a shoe length ahead. Both boots grounded, knees softly unlocked almost straight, centre of gravity comfortably over feet. Only a small natural hinge at the hips. Shoulders dropped, elbows comfortably near his sides, hands loose on the wood handle, a calm unforced expression as he looks toward his work. No deep bend, wide lunge, crouch, reaching for the foreground, or hand on his knee. Avoid an athletic or action pose. Keep John’s proportions, lean mature build and lightly greying beard true to the camera photos. To fit his more upright posture keep his head comfortably in frame: camera may pull back just enough, but dedicate the foreground to the action and do not add sky or shed. Place the rake much closer to his boots so its shaft can be fairly upright and his hands at comfortable waist and lower chest height. A short, light finishing stroke only, no stress or force. Choose a slightly side-on three-quarter stance so his body and both hands are readable.
RAKE GEOMETRY IS THE KEY TECHNICAL CORRECTION. It must be a real, modest-sized, rigid 12-tooth soil rake: a straight rectangular brown-grey iron crossbar roughly 30 cm wide, a row of equally spaced short steel teeth all facing DOWN, SIX TEETH on one side of the socket, SIX TEETH on the other. A single central metal tang/socket is welded to the EXACT GEOMETRIC MIDPOINT of the crossbar, in the gap between teeth 6 and 7. The wooden handle slots straight and concentrically into this single socket: extend the wooden handle axis visually down through the very middle of the metal ferrule and it meets the midpoint of the head, no offset bend, no T ending one-third in, no asymmetric side arm. Crossbar left and right halves project visibly the same distance from where the socket meets it, like the two equal arms of a balanced T. This is a typical 30cm rake head, only a little wider than one garden boot is long; slender 1.4 metre wooden shaft in proportion. Compose the rake head nearly broadside to the camera and close to horizontal in the image, with both end teeth and the middle attachment fully visible. Let the ground cover the very tips only, and keep a clear outline along the top edge so the joint can be judged. The central shaft comes from above and behind. NO leaf/fan rake, bow, offset side connection, enormous head, second handle, or surplus metal crosspieces. Small traces of dead grass caught on three or four teeth, strands continuing back into the patch, preserving its authentic pressed-down texture. Natural shadows not obscuring where shaft and head join. The strong physical legibility of this modest T-headed tool and relaxed ordinary gardening posture are the priority. No text or overlays, no second photo.

visual_research.source: University of Minnesota Turfgrass Science, Gary Deters, Figure 3
visual_research.observation: Direct lawn example after removing an opaque tarp: bare ground mixed with brown vegetation in irregular low patches. Some violets survived in this trial.

visual_research.source: Winterizing Garden Beds, Tarping to Reduce Tillage, p. 8
visual_research.observation: Three-frame bed sequence showing brown residual growth and exposed soil as the cover is pulled back.

edit: Central rake socket, smaller head and relaxed, upright stance.
